title: Is this process tailoring appropriate?
blurb: Judge whether a process, activity, workshop or artifact choice in a scenario still serves its purpose, and pick the reason that really explains the verdict.
question: Draycott Precision Engineering's project manager uses the 'controlling a stage' process during initiation to run a security review work package. Is this appropriate, and why?

teach.h: Tailor the how, keep the why
teach.body: The principle 'tailor to suit the project' asks the team to adapt PRINCE2 Agile to the project's size, complexity, risk and context: which agile frameworks, artifacts and workshops to use. Tailoring is agreed in initiation and recorded in the PID. A tailoring choice is appropriate when the process still achieves its purpose and each output is produced in the right place, by the right people. It is inappropriate when it defeats that purpose, however efficient it looks.

teach.h: Four checks for any process item
items: Name the process and activity, or the workshop and topic, the stem describes.
Recall that process's purpose and what the workshop is meant to achieve.
Check the output sits in the right workshop or topic and with the right role.
Choose the verdict, then the reason that explains THIS case, not just a true fact.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Easterholm County Council's Care Online
teach.body: Social workers have little time for workshops, so Simon Archer shortens the kickoff to half a day. He keeps psychological safety, team values, the skill and delegation matrices, and lets the digital team and practitioners design their own team dashboard. He records the change in the PID. Verdict: appropriate, because the kickoff still builds openness and self-management. Had he skipped the dashboards topic and imposed a template, the verdict would flip, because co-creation is the point.

teach.text: Traps: do not reject a choice simply because it differs from the book's default; reject it when it defeats the process purpose or moves an output to the wrong workshop or role. And do not pick a 'Yes' or 'No' option just because its reason is a true statement: it must explain the situation in the stem.

items: Tailoring is agreed in initiation and recorded in the PID.
Appropriate = purpose kept, output in the right workshop, right role.
Kickoff exists for openness and self-management; dashboards are co-created.
Controlling a stage may run in initiation for large or complex projects.
In BL4 items, reject reasons that are true but do not explain the case.

summary: You can now analyse whether a process, activity, workshop or artifact choice is fit for purpose in an agile scenario. You can also separate the reason that really explains a verdict from true statements that do not.

A.q: Pinewick Home and Garden's project initiation workshop reaches the 'management approaches' topic. The group uses this slot to list the criteria every user story must meet before development starts, such as clear requirements and known dependencies. Is this an appropriate application of the 'initiating a project' process, and why?
options: Yes, because the quality approach records agile ways of working
Yes, because the management approaches are co-created here
No, because readiness criteria belong in the project DoR topic
No, because readiness criteria are part of the project canvas
A.why: General criteria for starting work on stories are the project Definition of Ready topic; 'management approaches' covers overall governance such as risk, quality and change (Table 13.7).

whyNot.0: The quality management approach does record agile ways of working, but story readiness criteria have their own topic.
whyNot.1: Approaches are co-created in this workshop, but that does not make it the right topic for readiness criteria.
whyNot.3: The verdict is right but the reason is wrong: the canvas holds business justification, not readiness criteria.

A.q: Draycott Precision Engineering's initiation is unusually complex: sensors have a ten-week lead time and the IT security manager needs a review before any sensor connects. Andrea Lucas uses 'controlling a stage' during initiation to authorize work packages for the security review and a sensor trial. Is this an appropriate application of the processes, and why?
options: Yes, because controlling a stage may be used in a complex initiation
Yes, because initiating defines the scope, costs and decision structure
No, because controlling a stage begins after project authorization
No, because work packages are reserved for delivery stages
A.why: Controlling a stage is normally first used after the project is authorized, but it can be used during initiation, especially for large or complex projects (13.5.1).

whyNot.1: This describes initiating correctly, but it does not explain why controlling a stage can be used here.
whyNot.2: That is the normal pattern, not a rule; large or complex projects may use it during initiation.
whyNot.3: Work packages can be used in initiation when controlling a stage runs there, as it may for a complex project.

A.q: Easterholm County Council's board holds an agile enablement workshop in every stage, attended by board members, agile coach Gita Bhatt and representatives of social care operations, to reassess the Agilometer and plan responses to adoption risks. Is this an appropriate application of the 'directing a project' process, and why?
options: Yes, because the board approves the release map in this workshop
Yes, because it keeps agile maturity and risks under review
No, because the Agilometer is assessed once, in initiation
No, because the agile coach should hold it with the teams
A.why: The agile enablement workshop holds regular Agilometer assessments in initiation and later stages so agile maturity and agile risks are assessed regularly, for the board, agile coaches and business representatives (13.3.3).

whyNot.0: The release map is approved in 'authorize a stage or exception plan', not in the enablement workshop.
whyNot.2: The first project Agilometer is built in initiation, but it is reassessed regularly afterwards.
whyNot.3: This workshop is for the board, agile coaches and business representatives, not a team-level session.

B.q: Larkspur Rail's board uses its stage 2 agile enablement workshop to write an agile transformation plan to replace the change management approach. Is this an appropriate application of the processes, and why?
options: Yes, because the workshop links risks to transformation goals
Yes, because the executive approves the management approaches
No, because the plan comes from the project initiation workshop
No, because the plan should be written by the agile coach later
B.why: Where needed, the agile transformation plan replaces the change management approach as an output of the project initiation workshop's management approaches topic, not of the agile enablement workshop (Table 13.7, Table 13.5).

whyNot.0: The Agilometer review does link risk areas to transformation objectives, but it does not create the plan.
whyNot.1: The executive does approve management approaches, but that does not make this the right workshop.
whyNot.3: The verdict is right but the reason is wrong: the plan is produced in initiation, not later by the coach.

B.q: Callowmere University's web team holds its team planning workshop. After estimating, it selects stories for the sprint by priority and leaves out two Should have stories, because including them would make the team plan unrealistic. Is this an appropriate application of the 'managing product delivery' process, and why?
options: Yes, because iteration planning aims for a realistic team plan
Yes, because the CPO selects stories for each team's sprint
No, because every story in the work package must be delivered
No, because Should haves are fixed in PRINCE2 Agile scope
B.why: Iteration planning selects stories by priority and estimated effort to finalize a realistic team plan; the team plan shows what can be completed within the constraints (Table 13.13, Table 13.12).

whyNot.1: The CPO prioritizes across teams and owns the project backlog; the team selects its sprint stories.
whyNot.2: A team plan shows what can be completed within the constraints; not every story has to fit one sprint.
whyNot.3: Scope is fixed for Must haves and flexed for Should and Could haves.

B.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group holds a progress review workshop each month in stage 2. Board members review the project dashboard, and tenants' panel members try the photo reporting feature in a product demo and give feedback. Is this an appropriate application of the 'controlling a stage' process, and why?
options: Yes, because a progress review replaces the stage boundary
Yes, because reviews pair dashboard metrics with live demos
No, because demos are held in the project closure workshop
No, because tenants do not sit on the project board
B.why: The progress review workshop reviews project dashboard metrics and open risks and includes a product demo to gather user acceptance and feedback (13.5.4.1, Table 13.10).

whyNot.0: Progress reviews support controlling a stage; they do not replace the stage boundary decision.
whyNot.2: The closure workshop has a final demo, but progress reviews also demo completed features during stages.
whyNot.3: Board membership is irrelevant: users take part in demos to give feedback.

C.q: Pinewick Home and Garden's project is at the stage 2 boundary. Instead of a release planning workshop, Patrick Dunne and Marcus Lindell, the chief product owner, update the release map for stage 3 between them and email it to both teams. Is this an appropriate application of the 'managing a stage boundary' process, and why?
options: Yes, because the CPO prioritizes work across both teams
Yes, because the PM prepares the plan for the next stage
No, because the board should update the release map
No, because the teams should plan the stage together
C.why: The release planning workshop aligns the teams with the vision and plans the next stage collaboratively: OKRs, user stories and the release map (13.7.4.1, Table 13.16).

whyNot.0: The CPO does prioritize across teams, but that does not replace planning the stage with the teams.
whyNot.1: The PM does prepare the next stage plan, but PRINCE2 Agile does this through the collaborative workshop.
whyNot.2: The verdict is right but the reason is wrong: the board approves the release map, it does not update it.

C.q: Easterholm County Council's project is closing. Simon Archer drops the 'lessons report' topic from the project closure workshop, saying the council has no other agile projects planned. Is this an appropriate application of the 'closing a project' process, and why?
options: Yes, because lessons were captured in team retrospectives
Yes, because the end project report holds the lessons
No, because the topic sets actionable lessons for the future
No, because the board should write the lessons report
C.why: The lessons report topic defines actionable lessons for future projects, with Agilometer and psychological safety trends; lessons help the organization whatever its next project is (Table 13.19).

whyNot.0: Retrospectives capture lessons during the project, but the closure topic turns them into lessons for future projects.
whyNot.1: The end project report reviews performance; lessons go into the separate lessons report.
whyNot.3: The verdict is right but the reason is wrong: the PM and team prepare the lessons report.

C.q: Larkspur Rail is in starting up. Bronwen Hale, the project executive, leads the project canvas workshop from the mandate. In the starting up workshop, Rhys Pengelly creates the project backlog of epics with Matteo Ricci (CPO), Gemma Lowther (senior supplier) and Bronwen. Is this an appropriate application of the 'starting up a project' process, and why?
options: Yes, because the PM owns and prioritizes the project backlog
Yes, because these are the roles the activity names
No, because the project backlog is created in initiation
No, because the CPO should lead the project canvas
C.why: In 'prepare the outline business case' the executive leads the canvas from the mandate and the PM, with the CPO, senior supplier and executive, creates the project backlog in the starting up workshop (Table 13.1, Table 13.3).

whyNot.0: The CPO owns the project backlog; the PM leads its creation with the others.
whyNot.2: The project backlog with epics is an output of the starting up workshop; initiation may update it.
whyNot.3: The executive leads the canvas; the CPO represents users and owns the project backlog.

reteach.title: Adapting a family recipe
reteach.question: When you change a recipe to suit your kitchen, how do you know whether the change is fine or has ruined the dish?

blocks.h: Change the method, keep the dish
blocks.body: Swapping a fan oven for a gas oven, or halving the batch, is fine as long as the cake still rises: the purpose survives. Leaving out the raising agent, or adding it at the wrong step, defeats the purpose however quick it is. Judge PRINCE2 Agile tailoring the same way: does the process still do its job, with each output made at the right step by the right person?

blocks.text: 'Ovens vary in temperature' is true, but it does not tell you whether leaving out the raising agent is acceptable. In BL4 items, the reason must explain the case.

explain.body: In initiating, 'agree tailoring requirements' seeks lessons on how to tailor and defines the tailoring requirements as part of the PID. The principle 'tailor to suit the project' also asks for tailoring to be recorded in the PID.

test.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group decides that its service design team will keep its Kanban board and two-week iterations instead of Scrum sprints, and that the starting up workshop was shortened. The project is in initiation. Where should these tailoring decisions be recorded?
options: In the daily log
In the project canvas
In the issue register
In the PID
test.why: Tailoring requirements are agreed in initiation and recorded as part of the PID (Table 13.6, 5.2.1.7).

whyNot.0: The daily log records informal actions and notes, not the agreed way the project will be run.
whyNot.1: The project canvas holds the business justification, not how the method is tailored.
whyNot.2: The issue register records issues; tailoring decisions are not issues.

explain.body: The project kickoff workshop aligns the team and stakeholders on vision, objectives and scope, and builds teamwork. Through intros, psychological safety, values, skill matrices and co-created dashboards it creates an agile culture of openness and self-management.

test.q: At Callowmere University's project kickoff workshop, which of these choices BEST supports the workshop's purpose?
options: Each team agrees its own values and designs its own dashboard
The PM presents a finished delegation matrix for teams to sign
The PM assigns team values so both teams work the same way
The PM sets the skill matrix ratings from staff appraisals
test.why: The kickoff builds openness and self-management; teams agree their own values and co-create their dashboards (13.4.4.2, Table 13.8).

whyNot.1: A finished matrix handed down removes the team's part in agreeing how decisions are delegated.
whyNot.2: Imposed values do not build the team's own agile culture; values are co-decided.
whyNot.3: The skill matrix is completed collaboratively by the team, not set from appraisals.

explain.body: Personas are defined in the project initiation workshop; the project backlog with epics is created in the starting up workshop; team OKRs are set in the release planning workshop; improvement suggestions go to 'the learning' in a team retrospective.

test.q: Draycott Precision Engineering's project manager wants the engineers and software team to write a few fictional, needs-based personas of maintenance engineers to guide product decisions. In which workshop should this be done?
options: The project kickoff workshop
The release planning workshop
The team planning workshop
The project initiation workshop
test.why: Persona definition is a topic of the project initiation workshop (Table 13.7).

whyNot.0: The kickoff covers team intros, values, matrices and dashboards, not personas.
whyNot.1: Release planning covers OKRs and the release map for the next stage.
whyNot.2: Team planning prepares the next iteration's team plan.

explain.body: When an option's reason is a true statement about the method, ask whether it explains the situation. If the verdict would stand just as well without it, it is a distractor.

test.q: Coinbridge Payments receives Larkspur Rail's request for proposal and uses it to trigger starting up for its own delivery project. Is this an appropriate application of the 'starting up a project' process, and why?
options: Yes, because starting up asks if the project is worthwhile
Yes, because a mandate can be a request for proposal
No, because Larkspur's executive must issue the mandate
No, because a feasibility study is needed to start up
test.why: The mandate is whatever information triggers the project, such as a feasibility study or, in a supplier environment, a request for proposal (13.2.1).

whyNot.0: Starting up does ask that question, but it does not explain why an RFP can trigger the process.
whyNot.2: Coinbridge's own project is commissioned within Coinbridge; Larkspur's RFP is the triggering information.
whyNot.3: A feasibility study is one possible mandate, not a requirement.
